paper_a.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Double Q-learning

paper_b.title: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning

metadata.description: Paper A (Double DQN, van Hasselt et al. 2016) is a minimal modification of paper B (DQN, Mnih et al. 2013): it keeps the same network, replay buffer, and target-network machinery but replaces the bootstrap target $Y^{DQN}_t = R_{t+1}+\gamma\max_a Q(S_{t+1},a;\theta^-_t)$ with $Y^{DoubleDQN}_t = R_{t+1}+\gamma Q(S_{t+1},\arg\max_a Q(S_{t+1},a;\theta_t),\theta^-_t)$, decoupling action selection from evaluation to remove the positive bias of the max operator. Paper A explicitly cites and reuses paper B's DQN as a building block; the relation is most naturally an equivalence/translation (BI) where paper A's setup is a one-line dictionary change of paper B's, while paper A's overestimation theorems (TP244.1, TP244.2) are net new contributions with no counterpart in paper B.

matches.explanation: Both papers state a top-level RL problem on Atari, but at different abstraction levels. Paper B's problem is concretely 'learn Atari control from raw pixels'; paper A's problem is 'is overestimation by Q-learning under function approximation common, harmful, and fixable at scale?'. Paper A's problem presupposes paper B's setting (DQN on Atari) and refines it to a diagnostic/correction question, so they share a problem domain rather than a problem statement.

Both define the optimal action-value function $Q_*(s,a)=\max_\pi \mathbb{E}[\sum_{t}\gamma^t R_t|s_0=s,a_0=a,\pi]$. Paper A splits this into the policy-conditioned $Q_\pi$ (DP244.1) and its supremum $Q_*$ (DP244.2); paper B compresses both into DP238.4. Same standard MDP definition.

Both define a parameterized neural-network function approximator $Q(s,a;\theta)\approx Q_*(s,a)$. Identical concept; paper A uses bold $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, paper B uses plain $\theta$, but the object is the same Q-network.

Both define the DQN architecture as a CNN mapping a state (Atari frames) to a vector of action values, with one output per action. Paper B (DP238.9) gives the precise 1-conv1-conv2-FC-output architecture used originally; paper A (DP244.4) gives the abstract 'multi-layer NN $\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$' reformulation while explicitly citing Mnih et al. 2015. Same network in different levels of detail.

Both define experience replay: a memory of past transitions sampled uniformly to update the network and decorrelate consecutive samples. Paper A (DP244.6) explicitly cites Lin 1992 and Mnih et al. 2015; paper B (DP238.7) is the contribution that introduced it in the deep-RL setting.

Paper A defines the target network $\theta^-$ explicitly (DP244.5, cited from Mnih et al. 2015). Paper B (the 2013 NIPS-workshop DQN) does not yet contain a target-network mechanism — that was added in the 2015 Nature paper. So this concept is genuinely absent from paper B's graph and the unmatched-A entry is paper-relevant; we mark it as none with the caveat that it is cited-from-external in paper A (origin=external, but central enough that we surface it).

Both write the Q-learning gradient parameter update $\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t+\alpha(Y-Q(s,a;\theta))\nabla_\theta Q(s,a;\theta)$. Paper A presents it as the closed-form update with target $Y^Q_t$; paper B writes the corresponding loss gradient $\nabla_\theta L$. The two equations are the same SGD update on the squared TD error.

Bootstrap target / Bellman family. Paper B's Bellman EP238.1 ($Q^*(s,a)=\mathbb{E}[r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a')|s,a]$) and Q-learning loss target EP238.2 ($y_i=\mathbb{E}[r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a';\theta_{i-1})|s,a]$) are exactly paper A's Q-learning target EP244.2 ($Y^Q_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma\max_a Q(S_{t+1},a;\theta_t)$) and DQN target EP244.3 ($Y^{DQN}_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma\max_a Q(S_{t+1},a;\theta^-_t)$, distinguished only by using the target network). Composite many-to-many because the granularity differs: paper A separates the online vs target-network variants, paper B does not.

EP244.4 rewrites the Q-learning target as $R_{t+1}+\gamma Q(S_{t+1},\arg\max_a Q(S_{t+1},a;\theta_t);\theta_t)$ to make the selection/evaluation split explicit — algebraically identical to EP238.2 but reframed to motivate the Double Q decoupling. Same equation, different presentation; we mark analogous because the selection/evaluation phrasing is paper-A specific.

The Double Q-learning target $Y^{DoubleQ}_t$ (EP244.5, cited from van Hasselt 2010) and the Double DQN target $Y^{DoubleDQN}_t$ (EP244.6, paper A's main contribution) have no counterpart in paper B — paper B only defines the standard $\max$-over-actions bootstrap target. EP244.6 is the central contribution of paper A.

EP244.7 (running average value-estimate diagnostic over $T=125\,000$ steps) is paper A's tool for empirically detecting overestimation; paper B has no diagnostic of this form. (Paper B's ExP238.2 reports average max-Q on a held-out set, but as a stability sanity check, not as a bias diagnostic — see ExP244.3 ↔ ExP238.2 below.)
Normalized score (EP244.8) is paper A's reporting metric, cited from Mnih et al. 2015; the 2013 paper B reports raw scores against random / Sarsa / human, not normalized scores.

Paper A's two theorems on Q-learning overestimation — the Thrun-style tight lower bound $\max_a Q_t(s,a)\ge V_*(s)+\sqrt{C/(m-1)}$ (TP244.1) and the uniform-error expectation $(m-1)/(m+1)$ (TP244.2) — are paper-A original theoretical contributions. Paper B contains no theorems on overestimation; its only theorem is the cited convergence-of-value-iteration (TP238.1).

Paper B cites the convergence of value iteration $Q_i\to Q^*$ in the tabular finite-MDP setting (origin=external, Sutton & Barto). Paper A does not include this background result. Although external-origin nodes are usually exempt from `none` entries, paper B presents this as a load-bearing motivating theorem so we surface it.
Both proofs (lower-bound proof PP244.1 with steps PSP244.1-7, and uniform-error expectation proof PP244.2 with steps PSP244.8-11) exist only in paper A. Paper B has no proofs.
Both cite Watkins 1989 Q-learning as the underlying online TD algorithm. Identical external citation; same algorithm.

AP244.2 (DQN, cited from Mnih et al. 2015) and AP238.2 (Deep Q-learning with experience replay, paper B's main algorithm) are the same DQN algorithm in two presentations. Paper A treats DQN as a black-box building block to modify; paper B provides the full pseudocode, expanded into the algorithm_step children ASP238.1-7. The 2015-Nature target-network refinement (referenced in AP244.2 and DP244.5) is the only addition to paper B's 2013 version; we accept this as 'exact' on the central DQN object.
Tabular Double Q-learning (AP244.3, cited from van Hasselt 2010) is the algorithmic ancestor that paper A scales up; paper B precedes it in time and contains no double-estimator algorithm.

Composite L1+L2 alignment: paper A's Double DQN algorithm (AP244.4) and its four steps (ASP244.1-4: select with online net, evaluate with target net, gradient step, periodic target refresh) is the targeted modification of paper B's Deep Q-learning algorithm (AP238.2), specifically replacing the $y_j=r_j+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(\phi_{j+1},a';\theta)$ in ASP238.6 (and the corresponding gradient step ASP238.7) with the decoupled select-online / evaluate-target target. All other steps (replay init, episode loop, $\epsilon$-greedy, transition execution, replay storage) are inherited unchanged from paper B and are not re-listed in paper A's algorithm decomposition. We emit this composite per v2 §'Level-2 nodes' rule (parent first + many-to-many composite for the inner-step DAG difference).

Agent-environment interaction definition (action set, observation set, reward signal) is laid out in paper B's background. Paper A omits this MDP plumbing because it inherits the entire setting from DQN.

Paper B's state-sequence definition $s_t=x_1,a_1,\ldots,x_t$ (handling perceptual aliasing by treating histories as states) is specific to the partially-observed Atari setting and is not redefined in paper A.
Discounted return $R_t=\sum_{t'=t}^T\gamma^{t'-t}r_{t'}$ is in paper B's background; paper A folds the return into the $Q_\pi$ definition (DP244.1) without separately stating it.
Behaviour distribution $\rho(s,a)$ for off-policy sampling is a paper-B background object; paper A does not surface it explicitly.
Preprocessing function $\phi$ (gray-scale, downsample, crop, 4-frame stack) is a paper-B implementation detail. Paper A inherits it but does not redefine it.

Both look at the average max-Q estimate during Atari training. Paper B (ExP238.2 on Breakout/Seaquest) treats the smoothly increasing held-out max-Q curve as a stability indicator (no divergence). Paper A (ExP244.3 on six games) reuses the same kind of curve but contrasts it with the true discounted return of the learned policy to demonstrate that DQN's curve drifts upward (overestimation) while Double DQN tracks the truth. Same instrument, opposite framing; analogous fits best.

Atari benchmark experiments. Paper B (ExP238.1 setup + ExP238.4 results table) reports DQN raw scores on 7 games against Random/Sarsa/Contingency/HNeat/human. Paper A (ExP244.4 no-op evaluation + ExP244.5 human-starts) reports normalized scores on 49 games comparing DQN vs Double DQN vs tuned Double DQN. Same benchmark family (ALE Atari) and same measurement spirit (compare against baselines including human), scaled and re-purposed for the bias-correction story; analogous rather than exact because the protocols, metrics, and game sets differ.

Paper A's polynomial-fit overestimation experiment (ExP244.1) and i.i.d. Gaussian-error illustration (ExP244.2) are toy bias demonstrations supporting the overestimation theorems. Paper B contains no analogous toy experiments — it goes directly from background to Atari.

Paper B's Seaquest value-function visualization (predicted V tracks enemy / torpedo / disappearance) is an interpretability example unique to paper B; paper A does not include trajectory-level value visualizations.
